prompt: In Fisher's famous experiment, a lady claims she can tell whether milk or tea was poured first. She is given $8$ cups, $4$ of each kind in random order, and must pick out the $4$ milk-first cups. If she is only guessing, what is the probability she identifies all $4$ correctly?
hint: If she guesses, every way of choosing $4$ cups out of $8$ is equally likely, and only ONE of those ways is completely right.

hints.text: If she guesses, every way of choosing $4$ cups out of $8$ is equally likely, and only ONE of those ways is completely right.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with $4$ cups, $2$ milk-first. The ways to choose 2 of 4 are $\binom{4}{2} = 6$, and only one is right, so the chance is $\frac{1}{6}$. Same idea with 8 and 4.
Count the ways to choose $4$ cups from $8$: $\binom{8}{4} = \frac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5}{4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1}$.
$\binom{8}{4} = 70$, so the probability of a perfect guess is $\frac{1}{70} \approx 0.014$.

explanation: Because the cups were put in RANDOM order, a guesser is equally likely to pick any set of $4$ cups.
The number of possible sets is $\binom{8}{4} = \frac{8 \times 7 \times 6 \times 5}{24} = 70$, and exactly one set is the correct one.
So $P(\text{all 4 correct by guessing}) = \frac{1}{70} \approx 0.014$. When she got them all right, Fisher argued chance was a poor explanation: the first significance test.

alternativeExplanations.title: Pick the cups one at a time
steps: First pick: $\frac{4}{8}$ chance it is milk-first. Second: $\frac{3}{7}$. Third: $\frac{2}{6}$. Fourth: $\frac{1}{5}$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why randomization was the key
steps: If the cups had been lined up in a pattern, the lady might have cracked the pattern instead of tasting.
Random order means the ONLY way to beat $\frac{1}{70}$ reliably is real ability.
This is why every experiment randomizes: it makes chance the only alternative explanation, and chance can be computed.
